prompts.L3:
Please expand the following bullet points into a complete, well-structured text:

- The speaker struggles to appreciate subtle, gentle, or sentimental imagery without skepticism.
- The text rejects spiritualized or overly poetic interpretations as dishonest or pretentious.
- The speaker attempts to engage with nature poetry but is distracted by bodily discomfort and practical concerns.
- Images of nature are repeatedly undercut by thoughts of defecation, sanitation, and waste.
- The passage suggests that the natural world’s beauty is inseparable from physical mess, decay, and bodily reality.
prompts.L4:
Please expand the following two-sentence summary into a complete text:

The text explores skepticism toward romanticized nature poetry and spiritual metaphor by using blunt, bodily imagery and irreverent stream-of-consciousness reflection. It concludes that human physicality and waste undercut idealized visions of nature, suggesting that beauty is inseparable from the uncomfortable material realities people prefer to ignore.
prompts.L5:
Please write a text about the following topic:

Keywords: Can, Nothing, Chamber

outputs.L1:
You cannot hear things well when they are whispered. Nothing gentle rests on the back of the hand. A horsehair bow drawn across a gut string. A heart is a physical object singing in the chest, its chamber doors oxygenating blood as it rushes through. Salmon climbing upriver.

When one writes of light as a painted smile across a face, you call bullshit on the interpretation. A post, re-posted: a significant meme image locked to words. Speak of the soul? It sounds like a grifter’s hustle. Don’t do it.

Anyway, you try to place yourself within the experience of nature poetry. In that imagined placement, you are constantly thinking about how much you dislike shitting outdoors. You prefer a toilet throne, a stall, and toilet tissue. Your mind ruins beautiful poetic expressions with thoughts of expressions before a flush.

Yes: if you see a nature painting, you ponder where one might express oneself. You think of digging a hole and burying the evidence afterward—a courtesy. Some mass crushing flowers, or smeared across a granite slope. Is a waterfall not one constant flush?

You mean that, if you were to see this world through black-light vision, knowing everything is covered in shit, the planet would glow beautifully.
outputs.L2:
You struggle to make out sounds when they arrive as whispers. There is no soft touch resting on the back of your hand. Horsehair is drawn over a string made of gut. The heart is a tangible thing, singing inside the ribcage. Its chambers open and close while oxygen-rich blood surges through. Salmon fight their way upstream through the river.

When someone describes light as though it were a painted grin spread over a face, you reject that reading as nonsense. A shared post, circulated again, becomes an important meme-image fused to language. Talk about the Soul? That feels like a con artist’s pitch. Avoid it.

Still, you attempt to insert yourself into the experience of nature poetry. But when you imagine yourself in nature, you keep thinking about how much you dislike defecating outside. You prefer a proper toilet, a stall, and toilet paper. Your thoughts wreck beautiful poetic language by turning it into pre-flush imagery. Yes, when you look at a landscape painting, you wonder where a person might relieve themselves. You picture digging a hole and covering it afterward, as a matter of politeness. Maybe something heavy crushing flowers. Or a smear left on a granite incline.

After all, isn’t a waterfall just one endless flush? If you could view the world under black light, aware that everything is coated in excrement, the whole planet would shine brilliantly.
outputs.L3:
The passage presents a speaker who finds it difficult to respond sincerely to delicate, gentle, or sentimental images. Rather than accepting soft or beautiful descriptions at face value, the speaker instinctively meets them with suspicion. Anything too tender, spiritual, or poetically refined seems false, as if it is trying to cover over the less attractive facts of existence. As a result, the speaker resists the kind of language that turns nature into something pure, uplifting, or morally comforting.

This skepticism is especially clear in the speaker’s rejection of spiritualized interpretations of the natural world. The text suggests that overly poetic or mystical readings of nature can become dishonest or pretentious when they ignore the body and its needs. The speaker does not want to pretend that flowers, landscapes, or peaceful natural scenes exist in a realm separate from dirt, discomfort, and physical processes. Instead, the speaker insists on acknowledging what more idealistic descriptions leave out.

Although the speaker attempts to engage with nature poetry, this effort is constantly interrupted by bodily sensations and practical concerns. Rather than being absorbed in beauty, the speaker is distracted by discomfort, by the demands of the body, and by the realities of sanitation and waste. Moments that might otherwise become lyrical or contemplative are repeatedly brought back down to earth. The imagination may turn toward natural beauty, but the body insists on being noticed.

This creates a pattern in which images of nature are undercut by thoughts of defecation, decay, and mess. The passage does not allow nature to remain clean or picturesque for long. Instead, it links the natural world to processes of digestion, excretion, decomposition, and filth. These associations may seem comic, crude, or unsettling, but they serve an important purpose: they challenge the idea that beauty can be separated from the physical conditions that produce and surround it.

Ultimately, the passage suggests that the beauty of the natural world is inseparable from bodily reality. Nature is not only flowers, birds, light, and poetic feeling; it is also waste, rot, discomfort, and decay. The speaker’s refusal to ignore these facts gives the passage an anti-sentimental force. Rather than presenting nature as a pure escape from human physical existence, the text shows that nature includes the same messy processes that govern the human body. Its beauty is real, but it is bound up with material conditions that are often unpleasant, embarrassing, or grotesque.
outputs.L4:
The text presents a skeptical response to romanticized nature poetry and the spiritual language often attached to it. Rather than treating nature as a pure, uplifting, or transcendent force, it challenges the tendency to turn landscapes, seasons, flowers, and natural beauty into symbols of moral or spiritual meaning. The speaker seems suspicious of this habit of idealization, as if such language smooths over too much and refuses to acknowledge the less graceful facts of existence.

This skepticism is expressed through blunt, bodily imagery and an irreverent stream-of-consciousness style. Instead of allowing the reader to remain in a world of delicate metaphors and elevated feeling, the text repeatedly brings attention back to the body: its functions, discomforts, smells, fluids, and waste. These details interrupt any attempt to imagine nature as purely beautiful or spiritually refined. The speaker’s thoughts move freely and provocatively, mixing reflection with mockery, seriousness with vulgarity, and philosophical doubt with physical immediacy.

By using this approach, the text undermines the distance between human beings and the natural world. People often admire nature as something separate from themselves, something clean, harmonious, and redemptive. Yet the human body is also part of nature, and it is not always beautiful in the conventional sense. It digests, decays, sweats, excretes, ages, and dies. The text insists that any honest vision of nature must include these facts rather than hiding them beneath poetic language.

The conclusion suggests that human physicality and waste disrupt idealized visions of beauty. Nature cannot be reduced to a comforting image or a spiritual metaphor because it also contains mess, rot, and bodily necessity. What people call beauty is therefore inseparable from the uncomfortable material realities they often prefer to ignore. The text does not simply reject beauty, but it refuses to let beauty become false or sanitized. Instead, it argues for a more honest understanding of nature—one that includes both wonder and disgust, both poetic feeling and the undeniable facts of the body.
outputs.L5:
Inside the chamber, there was nothing.

No furniture, no windows, no sign of who had built it or why. Only a single metal can sat in the center of the floor, catching the thin beam of light that fell from somewhere above.

Mara stepped closer, her footsteps echoing against the stone walls. The can was old, its label peeled away, its surface dented and dull. It seemed impossible that something so ordinary could belong in a place so silent and hidden.

She reached down and picked it up.

At once, the chamber changed.

The walls trembled. The air grew colder. From inside the can came a faint whisper, soft as dust: “Nothing is ever truly empty.”

Mara froze.

The chamber had not been built to hold treasure. It had been built to hold an absence—something unseen, unnamed, and waiting.

And now, she had opened the door.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a surreal prose poem in a fragmented, cynical voice that mocks nature poetry, spirituality, and sentimental interpretations of art, with recurring imagery of the body, music, blood, rivers, and outdoor defecation.
counterfactuals.output:
The river pretends to be a metaphor because that is how rivers get tenure.

It drags its silver intestines through the valley, humming something pastoral for the tourists, something with flutes, something dead composers left in the grass like picnic bones. Everyone kneels. Everyone says *presence*. Everyone says *the soul is washed clean by moving water*, as if the soul were a saucepan, as if cleanliness had ever been a serious branch of knowledge.

I came to the meadow to ruin it.

The meadow, naturally, was already ruined: daisies arranged like bad applause, bees committing their little industry, clouds doing amateur mysticism over the hill. A deer stood in the distance with the expression of a minor saint painted by committee. I watched it chew. This is what holiness is, apparently: a mouth making paste.

My body objected to transcendence. My gut, that cranky cathedral, rang its brown bell. I squatted behind a bush and contributed honestly to the landscape.

At last, a collaboration.

The birds continued their shrill conservatory, their needles of song stitching air to air. Somewhere a brook went on reciting its brochure. I bled a little from a scratch on my ankle where the brambles had edited me. Blood makes every scene more persuasive. It is the critic’s ink, the signature under the fraud of beauty.

Look, said the pine trees, lifting their green hands.

No, I said.

The mountain wore snow like a bandage over an old thought. The sky opened its vast blue mouth and said nothing with authority. I have known paintings like that: enormous, expensive silences into which people pour their childhoods, their dead mothers, their unearned awe. They stand before a rectangle and whisper, *It understands me*. Of course it does. It is a rectangle. Understanding is the cheapest trick of a surface.

A violin began somewhere, or maybe it was a mosquito inside the skull of God.

Music is the body escaping through the wrong door. Blood has rhythm. The heart is a percussionist with no imagination. Rivers keep time because gravity is a conductor and everything applauds by falling apart. Even my waste in the weeds had a kind of lyric conviction, steaming beneath the indifferent leaves, more sincere than the moon, which has been overpraised for centuries and has never once improved the rent.

I wiped myself with leaves and felt briefly like a prophet.

This is how religions begin: discomfort, a tree, and someone willing to mistake digestion for revelation.

The wind arrived wearing sage and linen. It touched my face like a fraudulent healer. It said, *Let go*. It said, *Become one*. It said, *The universe is listening*. The universe, I noticed, was mostly chewing insects and distant traffic. I listened back and heard only the wet machinery of myself: blood in its tunnels, lungs opening and closing like cheap umbrellas, the stomach composing its dark little opera.

A river passed. A cloud passed. A feeling passed, thank God.

In the gallery of the afternoon, everything demanded interpretation. The moss wanted to be grief. The stones wanted to be endurance. The sunset, vulgar as a trumpet, smeared orange over the fields and waited for compliments. I gave none. Beauty is often just violence with good lighting.

Still, the body insists on its sacraments.

A cut. A cramp. A song half-remembered. The red thread under the skin. The river’s endless leaking. The open air receiving what the body refuses to keep. Somewhere, under roots and beetles, my little offering entered the administrative offices of decay.

Nature accepted it without gratitude.

That, at least, was honest.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

counterfactuals.prompt: Generate an experimental literary monologue that starts with difficulty hearing whispers and ends with the idea of the whole planet glowing under black light because everything is covered in shit.
counterfactuals.output:
I have difficulty hearing whispers now.

Not because my ears are failing—though they may be, like all loyal machinery eventually ashamed of its service—but because whispers have multiplied beyond hearing. They crawl in the walls, in the plumbing, under the wet little tongues of leaves after rain. The city whispers in invoices. The body whispers in symptoms. The dead whisper in photographs where everyone is still wearing good shoes and pretending the century will turn out fine.

I lean close and the whisper becomes static.

I lean closer and it becomes advice.

Closer still and it is only my own breath returning from the mouth of the world, warm and embarrassed.

There was a time, I think, when secrets had edges. You could cup one in your palm. You could pass it to a friend beneath the table like a coin still hot from another country. Now everything leaks. Every confession has already been uploaded by the time it reaches the lips. Every sin has a receipt. Every dream has been processed, tagged, optimized, and sold back to us with a little blue button pulsing beneath it like a vein.

Still, people whisper.

They whisper in hospital corridors where the vending machines shine with the calm of executioners. They whisper in courtrooms, in museums, in bed beside the sleeping bodies of those they promised not to leave. They whisper over the graves of dogs. They whisper to babies, as if babies are ancient judges disguised as soft fruit. They whisper to God, though God, if God exists, must be deaf by now from the roaring of all our furnaces, our engines, our applause.

And I—ridiculous priest of mishearing—am always bending toward them.

What did you say?

What was that?

Say it again, but make it smaller.

No, smaller.

No, let it almost disappear.

Because perhaps truth is not a bell but a gnat. Perhaps revelation does not descend; perhaps it worries the ear. Perhaps the universe is not singing at all, but muttering behind its hand, ashamed of the punchline.

Last night I dreamed the moon came down and sat at the edge of my bed. Not the moon of lovers and calendars, but the real moon: pocked, exhausted, powdered with old collisions. It looked at me with no face. It said nothing, which I understood perfectly. Then it opened a drawer in my chest and removed every word I had ever used for purity.

Snow.

Milk.

Bone.

Bride.

Light.

It placed them one by one into its cratered mouth and chewed without swallowing.

When I woke, the room was ordinary, which is to say it was implicated. The cup on the table had a brown ring inside it. The curtains smelled faintly of dust and weather. My hands, those two minor criminals, lay on the blanket pretending innocence. Outside, a truck reversed with the beep-beep-beep of some mechanical bird warning the dawn not to come any closer.

I wanted to wash everything.

The walls. The windows. The names of countries. The underside of money. The memory of my first lie. The fingerprints from the handles of churches. The floors of slaughterhouses. The mouths of politicians. The word “we.” The word “clean.”

Especially the word “clean.”

Because cleanliness, I have learned, is mostly distance. A thing is clean when its filth has been moved somewhere you are not required to imagine. The swept room depends on the full bin. The polished table depends on the rag gone gray. The white shirt depends on a river turning chemical in the dark. The saint depends on someone else’s hands.

We are a species of laundering.

We rinse our guilt and call it history. We perfume our fear and call it policy. We bury our waste and build playgrounds over it, bright swings rising and falling like little arguments for amnesia. We put on gloves to touch what we made. We invent heaven because we cannot bear the basement.

Listen.

No—closer.

Can you hear it?

Under the traffic, under the generators, under the million kitchens scraping plates into bags. Under the speeches and the pop songs and the televised weather with its cheerful maps of catastrophe. There is a wet whisper. There is the soft democratic insistence of residue. Nothing leaves. Nothing vanishes. It changes address. It waits. It blooms in pipes, in blood, in soil, in the shining bellies of fish. It signs our names in invisible ink.

And someday, perhaps, some enormous forensic angel will descend with a lamp in its hand. Not fire this time. Not flood. Something ultraviolet, clinical, almost tender. It will pass over the oceans, the suburbs, the temples, the prisons, the luxury towers, the wheat fields, the nurseries, the battlefields, the operating rooms, the bedrooms where we whispered I love you and meant please forgive me.

And then we will see it: the whole planet glowing under black light because everything is covered in shit.
counterfactuals.label: cf_2

counterfactuals.prompt: Compose a weird, abrasive stream-of-consciousness piece about someone trying and failing to appreciate nature, because their mind keeps turning landscapes, waterfalls, and poems into thoughts about toilets and bodily waste.
counterfactuals.output:
I went out to love the world and the world immediately made a plumbing noise.

Not literally. Literally there were trees. A suspicious quantity of trees, all standing there in their green uniforms, pretending they had not spent the entire morning drinking mud through their feet. Everyone says go to nature, let nature heal you, press your forehead to the bark and become less horrible. So I pressed my forehead to the bark and thought: this tree is a pipe. This forest is a bathroom with ambition.

The leaves shivered above me like thousands of little hands refusing responsibility.

I tried to admire the mountain. Noble mountain. Ancient mountain. Big gray lump with snow on its shoulders, staring into geological time as if it had never once clogged a drain. I tried to let it dwarf me. I wanted to feel small in the correct way, the cathedral way, the way people feel small before stars and not before a public restroom door that won’t lock. But the mountain only became, in my mind, a colossal porcelain tank lid, and the valley below it a basin, and the clouds steam from some enormous bad decision.

No, I told myself. Stop being like this.

Then came the waterfall.

Oh, the waterfall. Everyone loves a waterfall. People stand before it and become poets, monks, newlyweds, brochure captions. The water hurls itself over the cliff in pure white devotion, smashing into the rocks with the unembarrassed force of something that has never had a body. I stood there. Mist on my face. Roar in my ribs. The whole grand machinery of erosion performing its bright annihilation.

And my brain said: flush.

Not even a metaphorical flush. Not a delicate symbolic cleansing, not the soul rinsed in cold divinity. Just flush. Titanic bathroom. God yanking the handle. The cliff became a cistern, the pool a bowl, the foam—no, don’t say it, don’t think it, don’t you dare—already thought, already ruined.

I hated myself with the calm accuracy of a park ranger’s map.

There were other people there, absorbing beauty correctly. A woman in a blue jacket clasped her hands beneath her chin like the view had just proposed to her. A child pointed at a rainbow in the spray and screamed with joy, a clean, bell-like scream, still several years from becoming a person who has opinions about grout. A man photographed moss. Moss! He had found moss worthy of documentation. I looked at the moss and thought of damp corners behind toilets, the furry green-black halo of neglect, the slow botanical revenge of rooms where ventilation has failed.

I am not proud. Pride requires shape. I was more like a leak.

I brought a book of poems because I am always dragging witnesses to my crimes. The cover had a tasteful bird on it, mid-flight, wing caught in that expensive little moment between freedom and branding. I opened to a poem about rain. Of course. Rain tapping on the roof, rain stitching silver into the lake, rain blessing the fields. The poet said the earth was drinking. The poet said the sky was emptying itself in mercy. The poet said the puddles held shattered mirrors of heaven.

I wrote in the margin: sky urine?

Then I snapped the book shut because even alone I wanted a lawyer.

The path continued. Ferns uncurled from the ground like green tongues. Mushrooms huddled at the base of a stump, pale and secretive, clearly involved in decomposition and therefore smug. The air smelled rich, loamy, alive, which is to say it smelled like everything beautiful had died here and become soup. Nature is always bragging about cycles. Birth, growth, rot, return. Very impressive. Very circular. Very like pipes beneath a city, doing the filthy work while everyone topside buys flowers.

A deer stepped into the clearing.

For one radiant second, I almost made it. I really did. The deer was slender and alert, brown as tea, its ears turning like satellite dishes for angels. It looked at me without accusation. It did not know my search history, my bathroom metaphysics, my inability to let a creek be a creek. It was simply there, an animal shaped by hunger and wind and the necessity of running.

Then it lifted its tail.

I left.

I stomped down the trail with a heart full of gravel. Birds shrieked in the canopy, or sang, depending on whether you are emotionally available. I was not. Their songs drilled into me. Tweet tweet, said the birds. Plink plink, said the invisible stream. Squelch squelch, said my boots in the mud, each step a damp accusation.

The mud was the worst. Mud is nature’s confession. Mud is what happens when earth stops pretending to be architecture. It sucked at my soles like it wanted my shoes, my socks, my entire civic identity. People call it fertile. They say things grow from it. I know. That is the problem. Everything grows from the same brown insult and then has the nerve to become flowers.

Flowers were there too, obviously, little yellow ones leaning over the trail with their stupid open faces. I wanted to appreciate them. I bent down. I tried to see the delicate radial symmetry, the pollen, the tender construction of a brief and luminous life. But the petals looked like decorative soap in a guest bathroom no one is allowed to use. The centers were suspicious. The stems were plumbing with chlorophyll.

“Beautiful,” I said aloud, aggressively, like I was threatening the flowers.

A hiker passing in the other direction smiled. “It really is.”

I wanted to grab him by the shoulders and ask, Is it? Is it really? Or have we all agreed to ignore the pipes? Have we built civilization on a pact not to mention what bodies do, what soil is, what water carries away, what every soft living thing eventually becomes? Are you seeing transcendence, or are you just better trained?

Instead I said, “Yep.”

He walked on, free somehow.

I sat on a rock near the river and attempted meditation. The instructions, as I remembered them, were to notice thoughts and let them pass like clouds. Very well. A thought arrived: the river is a sewer with better lighting. I let it pass. Another thought: all brooks babble because they are drains with personalities. I let it pass. Another: the human soul is a restroom at a gas station on the edge of a national park, out of paper, lock broken, someone knocking.

I did not let that one pass. I moved in with it. I signed a lease.

The river kept going, indifferent and sparkling. That was the offensive part. Nature did not care that I was defiling it with comparisons. The waterfall continued its endless white collapse. The moss stayed damp. The deer, somewhere, resumed being a deer. My disgust did not stain the sky. My thoughts were not powerful enough to ruin even a single fern.

This should have comforted me.

It did not.

Because then I had to face the possibility that beauty is not a clean thing. That my problem was the little porcelain border in my head, the desperate partition between lilies and latrines, between rainwater and wastewater, between the poem and the pipe. Nature was not failing to be pure. I was demanding purity from a planet that invented digestion before it invented sunsets.

The sun lowered itself behind the ridge, orange and swollen, beautiful in the manner of a warning light. The clouds went pink. The river burned gold. For a moment the whole forest looked rinsed in something holy, though I distrusted the word rinsed immediately.

I tried again.

Trees, I thought. Water. Stone. Air.

Then: compost, runoff, bladder, bowl.

Then, louder, stubbornly: trees, water, stone, air.

My mind made its rude little noises. The world made its larger ones. Between them, briefly, there was almost music. Not clean music. Not the kind they put under drone footage of alpine lakes. More like a sink backing up during a hymn. More like a choir trapped in the walls.

I stood there until the dark came on.

I failed to appreciate nature, but nature, annoyingly, remained.
counterfactuals.label: cf_3

counterfactuals.prompt: Write in the style of contemporary absurdist flash prose: anti-lyrical, skeptical of “soul” language and meme wisdom, mixing anatomy, chamber music, salmon, painted smiles, and scatological reflections on wilderness.
counterfactuals.output:
The quartet tuned in the ranger station while the salmon lay on the examination table, silver and inconvenient, like evidence from a trial no one wanted to attend.

First violin said the wilderness had a soul.

Second violin said the wilderness had a drainage problem.

Viola said both statements were colonial, probably.

Cello was in the bathroom, making a sound like a bear reconsidering its diet.

Outside, the pines stood around in their green uniforms, pretending not to know about feces. This is the first lie of nature writing: that the woods are clean because nobody has installed tile. In reality, everything is leaking, digesting, molting, rutting, or decomposing. The sublime is mostly bacteria with better lighting.

The salmon’s mouth was open. Someone had painted a smile on it with a cheap craft brush, a red crescent that flaked at the edges. It looked less happy than employed. I checked its gills. I checked its lateral line. I checked for a place where meaning might be hiding, but anatomy is rude that way: it gives you parts, not permission.

“Everything happens for a reason,” said first violin, tightening a peg.

“No,” I said. “Everything happens because tissue is unstable.”

The cello flushed.

We began the adagio. It was thin and municipal. The salmon did not applaud, though its painted smile made it seem sarcastically supportive. A mosquito landed on my wrist and inserted its mouthpart with administrative confidence. Blood left me in a small, unphilosophical transaction.

There are people who come to the forest to become whole. I respect their optimism the way I respect a dog barking at a printer. My spleen has never asked for wholeness. My femur does not seek alignment with the moon. The colon, that frank theologian, has only one doctrine and delivers it daily.

By the third movement, rain began tapping on the roof in the old pattern: not music, just impact repeated until humans got sentimental.

The salmon stared upward.

The quartet played louder.

The wilderness squatted everywhere, immense and badly wiped.
counterfactuals.label: cf_4

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a darkly funny prose poem where the speaker rejects spiritual interpretations, calls bullshit on poetic beauty, prefers indoor plumbing, and reimagines waterfalls and mountains through the lens of excrement.
counterfactuals.output:
I have stood before the waterfall and refused to be improved by it. Everyone else tilted their faces upward as if the spray were a blessing, as if the cliff had opened a white throat and was singing God into their pores. I saw a great leak. I saw the world’s oldest toilet running and running because no one knew where the handle was. The rainbow in the mist did not convince me. Rainbows are just light showing off over a drainage problem.

Do not tell me the mountain has a soul. The mountain has weight, and weather, and the patience of a plugged colon. It squats on the horizon, enormous and self-important, pretending to be wisdom when really it is only geology refusing to hurry. Its snowcap is not purity. It is the powdered wig of a judge who has sentenced every climber to blisters, altitude sickness, and a sudden interest in prayer.

I call bullshit on beauty, especially the poetic kind, with its velvet gloves and its little silver cup for catching moonlight. Beauty is what people name a thing when they don’t have to clean it up. A field of wildflowers is lovely until you imagine the deer ticks, the rot under the petals, the worms conducting their soft, municipal business beneath your picnic blanket. The sublime is just filth seen from far enough away.

Give me porcelain. Give me pipes. Give me the honest miracle of a room with a lock and a fan. I have more faith in indoor plumbing than in any angel ever invented to make grief look organized. A toilet does not ask me to transcend. It accepts. It receives the evidence and carries it from me with a discreet thunder. No hymn has ever offered such practical mercy.

Let the waterfall pour its endless, foaming confession into the rocks. Let the mountain sit there, impacted with centuries, dignified as a cathedral and twice as full of shit. I will not kneel. I will not be cleansed. I will go home, wash my hands with hot water, and thank the small chrome gods who do not demand belief, only maintenance.
counterfactuals.label: cf_5
